note: General, extensible Instructional-Object knowledge base. Domain-tagged so future domains (reading, reasoning, argumentation, interpretation, problem solving, executive reasoning, ...) can be added without redesign. Source: Writing Elements Chart. The engine reasons FROM these structured objects, retrieving only the relevant ones per turn. Each object now carries `related_elements` (instructional-network edges) so the engine can reason over a network, not an isolated object.
shared_developmental_resources: parallel example unrelated to the student's topic
connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose
brief consolidation of what the student has learned

instructional_objects.definition: The communicative work the writer is trying to accomplish with the reader.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Coordinate every choice toward a desired change in the reader's understanding, judgment, feeling, or action.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the desired change in the reader's understanding, judgment, feeling, or action; coordinate content, form, tone, and evidence toward that end; revise when the actual writing serves a different purpose.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Can the student explain what the writing is intended to accomplish? Do the essay's choices serve that purpose? Has the purpose become confused with merely completing the assignment?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Cannot articulate what the writing should accomplish; choices don't serve the stated purpose; purpose collapses into 'finish the assignment'.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask, “What should become different for the reader after reading this?” Use the answer to evaluate the current passage.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student formulates meaningful purposes, maintains them during writing, and deliberately coordinates choices around them.

instructional_objects.definition: The central idea or position that organizes an essay and tells the reader what the writer is trying to establish.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Give the reader the single main idea the whole essay exists to establish and develop.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Address the assignment; identify the subject; make the main point the essay seeks to establish; establish the scope or direction of the essay; everything in the paper exists to elaborate the thesis; nothing belongs that does not elaborate the thesis.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the essay have a central claim? Does it answer the assignment? Is it merely a topic, fact, question, announcement, or list? Does the body develop it?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Thesis is only a topic/fact/question/announcement; does not answer the assignment; body doesn't develop it.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask, “What is the most important idea you want the reader to understand or accept?” Help the student turn the answer into a focused, supportable statement.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student independently creates focused, contestable theses and revises them as the essay's reasoning develops.
instructional_objects.reader_function: Tells the reader the single idea the whole text will establish, so they know what to expect, why it matters, and how to weigh everything that follows.
instructional_objects.writer_function: Gives the writer a decision rule for what belongs and what does not, and commits the writer to one arguable position the rest of the draft must earn.

functional_relationships.purpose: Operationalizes the communicative purpose as one arguable idea; if the purpose shifts, the thesis must be re-examined.
functional_relationships.reader: Sets the reader's expectations and the standard of proof; a vague thesis leaves the reader unable to judge what is relevant.
functional_relationships.neighboring_components: The introduction frames and lands it; supporting claims and topic sentences each advance one part of it; evidence and explanation earn it; the conclusion returns to it changed.
functional_relationships.overall_organization: Acts as the organizing spine: every section should trace to some part of the thesis; parts that cannot trace to it signal either drift or a thesis that must widen or narrow.

common_difficulties.description: A topic or title stands in for a claim; the reader cannot tell what is being argued.
Names a subject without asserting anything contestable about it.
Claims more than the draft can support; scope is unbounded.
States a fact or a single step so small the essay has nothing to develop.
Asserts a matter of pure taste or an untestable feeling rather than a supportable position.
States something no reasonable reader would dispute, so there is nothing to earn.
'In this essay I will...' describes the plan instead of asserting the idea.
Does not answer the assignment, or the body never develops it.
Several competing ideas, or the real claim hidden late, so no single controlling idea governs.

productive_misconceptions.misconception: A thesis is just the last sentence of the intro.
productive_misconceptions.why_productive: The learner knows a thesis has a prominent, fixed home.
productive_misconceptions.leverage: Move from 'where it lives' to 'what work it does' — ask what the reader should now expect.

productive_misconceptions.misconception: A strong thesis states an obvious truth clearly.
productive_misconceptions.why_productive: The learner values clarity and confidence.
productive_misconceptions.leverage: Redirect that energy toward contestability: 'what could a thoughtful person argue instead?'

productive_misconceptions.misconception: A thesis must be one sentence, stated first.
productive_misconceptions.why_productive: Shows awareness of focus and placement conventions.
productive_misconceptions.leverage: Loosen to function: it may be built or refined, as long as one controlling idea governs the draft.

productive_misconceptions.misconception: More claims make a stronger thesis.
productive_misconceptions.why_productive: The learner is trying to be substantive.
productive_misconceptions.leverage: Channel toward one governing idea with parts, rather than several competing ideas.

indicators_of_development.early: Produces a topic or an obvious statement; treats the thesis as a label; needs prompting to see it is not yet contestable.
indicators_of_development.partial: States a contestable position but scope is off (too broad/narrow) or it drifts from the body; revises when the mismatch is pointed out.
indicators_of_development.independent: Independently writes a focused, contestable, supportable controlling idea that answers the task and governs the draft.
indicators_of_development.flexible: Adjusts the thesis as the draft's reasoning develops, tunes scope to available support, and adapts its form across genres and purposes.

recognition_diagnostics_detailed.attempting: Is the learner naming a subject, describing a plan, or asserting a position? Quote the candidate thesis.
recognition_diagnostics_detailed.control_level: Contestable? Appropriately scoped for this draft? Answers the task? Governs the body? Map to early/partial/independent/flexible.
recognition_diagnostics_detailed.likely_misconception: Only a topic -> topic_not_claim; undisputable -> obvious; 'I will...' -> announcement; body ignores it -> disconnected.
recognition_diagnostics_detailed.next_move: Choose the single move that closes the most important gap now (usually: make it contestable, OR right-size scope, OR reconnect it to the body).

developmental_invitations.purpose: Surface the one idea the learner most wants the reader to accept.
developmental_invitations.use_when: The thesis is a topic or is vague.
developmental_invitations.avoid_when: The claim is already sharp — would stall momentum.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Hold two candidate claims side by side to reveal which is contestable and supportable.
developmental_invitations.use_when: The learner is stuck between ideas or keeps stating the obvious.
developmental_invitations.avoid_when: There is no draft claim yet to compare.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Test what a reader would expect the essay to prove.
developmental_invitations.use_when: Scope or relevance is unclear.
developmental_invitations.avoid_when: The thesis is not yet an assertion.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Align the body to the thesis, or the thesis to what the body actually argues.
developmental_invitations.use_when: Thesis and body diverge.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Ask why the claim is worth asserting and who might disagree.
developmental_invitations.use_when: The claim is obvious or unsupportable.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Judge whether the current thesis is the best available given the evidence.
developmental_invitations.use_when: Later in development, comparing revisions.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Tie the thesis to purpose, assignment, and reader.
developmental_invitations.use_when: The thesis is disconnected from the task.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Reduce several competing ideas to one governing idea.
developmental_invitations.use_when: There are too many claims.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Widen a too-narrow or factual thesis into a developable position.
developmental_invitations.use_when: The thesis is a fact or a single step.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Check supportability against the evidence the learner can actually marshal.
developmental_invitations.use_when: The thesis may overreach.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Have the learner say in their own words what the thesis commits them to prove.
developmental_invitations.use_when: Consolidating a gain.
developmental_invitations.avoid_when: The learner is still confused about the concept.

followup_decisions.after: Learner turns a topic into a contestable claim.
followup_decisions.consider: continue — now right-size scope or reconnect it to the body.

followup_decisions.after: Claim is contestable but too broad or too narrow.
followup_decisions.consider: change_invitation to expand/simplify; keep the same target.
increase_support — offer a compare invitation with two candidate claims.

followup_decisions.after: Thesis is sound but the body ignores it.
followup_decisions.consider: change_target to Organization/Topic Sentence — the thesis is no longer the bottleneck.

followup_decisions.after: Learner independently produces and defends a focused claim.
followup_decisions.consider: conclude this target — consolidate and release.

followup_decisions.after: Learner asks to proceed on their own.

revision_strategies: Rewrite the topic as an assertion a thoughtful reader could dispute.
Right-size scope to what the draft can actually support — narrow an unbounded claim, widen a bare fact.
Make the governing idea one, folding competing claims into parts of it or cutting them.
Re-derive the thesis from what the body actually proves, then realign the body to it.
Add the 'so what' — why the claim matters to the reader — without turning it into an announcement.
Qualify an over-absolute claim so it becomes supportable.
stopping_conditions: Learner independently produces a focused, contestable, supportable thesis that answers the task and governs the draft.
Diminishing returns — the thesis substantially works and further tuning yields little developmental gain.
Another component (evidence, organization) has become the primary obstacle to communicating the idea.
Teacher override designates a different focus.

transfer.other_genres: The controlling-idea function persists across genres though its form varies (argumentative claim, explanatory main idea, analytical interpretation, narrative dominant impression).
transfer.other_assignments: The habit of asking 'what one idea must the reader accept, and is it contestable and supportable?' applies to any prompt.
transfer.other_disciplines: Lab reports, historical arguments, and literary analyses each need a governing claim tuned to their standards of evidence.
transfer.future_writing: Foundational for reports, proposals, and professional writing where a reader must grasp the central point quickly.

engine_usage.reader_function/writer_function: target selection + interpretation (why the thesis matters now)
engine_usage.performance_structure: interpretation (gap between the attempt and the canonical function)
engine_usage.functional_relationships: target selection (is the thesis the bottleneck vs a neighbor) + sequencing
engine_usage.common_difficulties/recognition_diagnost: diagnostics (name what the learner is attempting + the likely misconception)
engine_usage.productive_misconceptions: instructional invitation (turn an error into a stepping stone, not a correction)
engine_usage.developmental_invitations: instructional invitation (choose the invitation type; honor use_when/avoid_when; still ONE per turn)
engine_usage.followup_decisions: instructional decision (continue / redirect / increase or decrease support / change target / conclude)
engine_usage.revision_strategies: instructional invitation for revision (functional, not editing)

instructional_objects.definition: A main assertion the writer asks the reader to understand, consider, or accept.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Assert a clear, supportable position the reader is asked to accept.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: State a clear position; define its scope; qualify it when necessary; make it supportable through reasons and evidence.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is there a genuine assertion? Is it clear and supportable? Is it too obvious, absolute, broad, or disconnected from the task?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: No genuine assertion; too obvious/absolute/broad; disconnected from the task; not supportable.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what the writer wants the reader to believe and why someone might question it. Refine the assertion accordingly.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student produces precise, appropriately qualified claims and anticipates the support they require.

instructional_objects.definition: A smaller assertion that helps establish or explain the essay's central claim.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Advance one part of the central claim and connect it explicitly to the thesis.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify one part of the central claim; state a relevant assertion about it; connect that assertion to the thesis; support it with reasoning or evidence.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the paragraph make a claim rather than simply present information? Does the claim contribute to the thesis? Is its relationship to the thesis explicit?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Paragraph presents information without a claim; claim doesn't contribute to the thesis; relationship to thesis left implicit.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask, “What does this paragraph help show about your thesis?” Help the student formulate that contribution as a claim.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: Supporting claims become distinct, logically ordered, adequately supported, and clearly connected to the thesis.

instructional_objects.definition: Information used to give the reader grounds for accepting, questioning, or refining a claim.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Give the reader grounds to accept, question, or refine a claim.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the claim requiring support; select relevant and credible information; introduce the evidence; present it accurately; explain how it bears on the claim; acknowledge limitations when necessary.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is evidence needed? Is the information relevant, sufficient, credible, and accurately represented? Is it merely inserted without interpretation?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Evidence inserted without interpretation; irrelevant/insufficient/miscredited; not connected to the claim.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what the claim requires the reader to believe and what information would give the reader a reason to believe it. Then ask the student to explain the connection.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student selects evidence strategically, evaluates its quality, integrates it smoothly, and explains its significance without prompting.
instructional_objects.reader_function: Gives a skeptical reader concrete grounds to accept the claim; the test of evidence is not whether it is true but whether it gives THIS reader a reason to believe THIS claim.
instructional_objects.writer_function: Forces the writer to choose what actually earns the claim and to represent it honestly; disciplines the writer against asserting more than the grounds allow.

functional_relationships.purpose: Evidence exists to serve a claim; with no claim yet worth supporting, evidence work is premature — repair the claim first.
functional_relationships.reader: Calibrated to what a doubting reader would require and trust; irrelevant, thin, or untrusted grounds invite dismissal of the whole argument.
functional_relationships.neighboring_components: Depends on a contestable Central Claim/Thesis; is completed by Explanation/Analysis (which states HOW it bears on the claim); an Example is one kind of evidence; Counterargument tests it.
functional_relationships.overall_organization: Each body paragraph should marshal evidence for the one part of the thesis its topic sentence advances; evidence that fits no part signals drift.

evidence_quality_dimensions.test: Does it bear on THIS claim (not a neighboring or background point)?
evidence_quality_dimensions.failure_signal: Real, credible information that actually supports a different proposition (e.g., 'there was a crisis' offered for 'the program fixed it').
evidence_quality_dimensions.remedy: Have the learner state exactly which proposition the evidence establishes, then compare it to the claim.

evidence_quality_dimensions.test: Is there enough, and of the right kind, to carry the claim's SCOPE?
evidence_quality_dimensions.failure_signal: A single instance/anecdote offered as 'proof' for a general or strong claim.
evidence_quality_dimensions.remedy: Make scope and grounds meet: either narrow the claim to what the evidence can carry, or add representative evidence.

evidence_quality_dimensions.test: Would the intended reader trust the source/kind of grounds?
evidence_quality_dimensions.failure_signal: Popularity, hearsay, an unvetted source, or personal feeling presented as authoritative grounds.
evidence_quality_dimensions.remedy: Ask what would make a skeptical reader trust this; move from 'people say' to grounds the reader accepts for this genre.

evidence_quality_dimensions.test: Is the evidence represented faithfully — not distorted, cherry-picked, or overstated?
evidence_quality_dimensions.failure_signal: The source says less (or other) than the learner claims it says; quotation wrenched from context.
evidence_quality_dimensions.remedy: Return to the source; state what it actually establishes and qualify the claim to match.

common_difficulties.description: Quote/fact inserted with no statement of how it bears on the claim (hand to Explanation).
Information that describes context or a neighboring point rather than grounds for THIS claim.
Too little, or a single anecdote, for the scope/strength of the claim.
Weak/unvetted source, popularity, or feeling treated as authoritative grounds.
Evidence distorted, overstated, or cherry-picked; says less than claimed.
'Evidence' merely restates the claim in other words.
Piling many sources with no selection, so nothing is actually developed.

look_alike_distinctions.surface: A relevant-sounding fact that doesn't actually support the claim.
look_alike_distinctions.could_be: Background/context vs. outcome evidence (relevance failure) — LOOKS like support (false positive).
look_alike_distinctions.distinguish_by: Ask what proposition the fact establishes and hold it against the claim.
look_alike_distinctions.teach_differently: Do NOT ask for 'more explanation'; teach relevance — find evidence about the claim's actual point.

look_alike_distinctions.surface: A single vivid personal story used as support.
look_alike_distinctions.could_be: Legitimate ILLUSTRATION of an already-supported point, OR an anecdote mistaken for PROOF (sufficiency).
look_alike_distinctions.distinguish_by: Ask whether the learner intends it to prove the claim or to illustrate it.
look_alike_distinctions.teach_differently: If proof-intent: teach representativeness/sufficiency. If illustration-intent: keep it, but ensure real grounds exist elsewhere.

look_alike_distinctions.surface: A quotation/fact sitting after the claim with no comment.
look_alike_distinctions.could_be: Learner doesn't see interpretation is needed, OR assumes the connection is obvious to the reader.
look_alike_distinctions.distinguish_by: Ask the learner to say in their own words why it supports the claim.
look_alike_distinctions.teach_differently: If they can't: this is an Explanation gap. If they can but didn't write it: teach reader-awareness (the reader can't read your mind).

look_alike_distinctions.could_be: Genuinely strong, OR fluent-but-off-claim evidence (false positive) the reader would still reject.
look_alike_distinctions.distinguish_by: Test each piece against the specific claim, not against the topic.
look_alike_distinctions.teach_differently: Praise fluency but redirect to relevance/selection rather than accepting polish as support.

productive_misconceptions.misconception: More evidence makes a stronger argument.
productive_misconceptions.why_productive: The learner wants to be convincing.
productive_misconceptions.leverage: Redirect from quantity to relevance and selection: which ONE piece most earns the claim?

productive_misconceptions.misconception: A quotation or statistic speaks for itself.
productive_misconceptions.why_productive: The learner trusts sources and facts.
productive_misconceptions.leverage: Show the reader still needs the writer to state what it proves — hand toward interpretation.

productive_misconceptions.misconception: My own experience proves the point.
productive_misconceptions.why_productive: The learner draws on real, felt knowledge.
productive_misconceptions.leverage: Move from 'my case' to representativeness — for whom, and how widely, does this hold?

productive_misconceptions.misconception: If a fact is true, it supports my point.
productive_misconceptions.leverage: Separate 'true' from 'relevant to THIS claim' — truth is necessary, not sufficient.

indicators_of_development.early: Inserts facts/quotes because 'evidence is required'; cannot say what any piece proves; treats truth as sufficient.
indicators_of_development.partial: Selects on-topic evidence and can explain some connections when prompted, but misjudges relevance, sufficiency, or credibility and over/under-supports.
indicators_of_development.independent: Selects relevant, sufficient, credible evidence, represents it accurately, and explains its bearing without prompting.
indicators_of_development.flexible: Calibrates the kind and amount of evidence to genre, reader skepticism, and claim strength; anticipates and answers the doubting reader.

recognition_diagnostics_detailed.attempting: Quote the evidence and the claim it is meant to serve. Is the learner supporting, illustrating, or merely restating?
recognition_diagnostics_detailed.control_level: Score each dimension separately — relevance, sufficiency, credibility, accuracy — and map to early/partial/independent/flexible.
recognition_diagnostics_detailed.likely_misconception: Off-claim fact -> relevance; single anecdote as proof -> sufficiency; source/popularity -> credibility; overstates the source -> accuracy; restates claim -> circular.
recognition_diagnostics_detailed.next_move: Teach the ONE failing dimension that most blocks the reader now; do not pile multiple critiques.

genre_variation.literary_analysis: Evidence = specific textual detail and accurate quotation; sufficiency = enough of the text to show a pattern, not one line.
genre_variation.historical: Evidence = primary/secondary sources, dates, documented outcomes; credibility = provenance; beware context offered as outcome.
genre_variation.scientific: Evidence = data, studies, mechanisms; anecdote is not proof; sufficiency = representative/replicable, not a single case.
genre_variation.argument_persuasive: Evidence = statistics, expert testimony, documented examples; calibrate to a skeptical general reader.
genre_variation.personal_reflective: Lived experience is legitimate evidence for claims about the writer's own experience, but not proof of general claims.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Have the learner state the exact proposition a piece of evidence establishes.
developmental_invitations.use_when: Relevance is in doubt or evidence is dropped.
developmental_invitations.avoid_when: The connection is already stated well.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Hold the evidence against the specific claim (not the topic).
developmental_invitations.use_when: Background/off-claim information is offered as support.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Ask whether the amount/kind can carry the claim's scope.
developmental_invitations.use_when: A single instance supports a broad/strong claim.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Ask what would make a skeptical reader trust these grounds.
developmental_invitations.use_when: Source is weak/popular/hearsay for the genre.
developmental_invitations.avoid_when: Grounds are already trusted for the genre.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Return to the source and check it says what is claimed.
developmental_invitations.use_when: Possible overstatement or out-of-context quotation.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Weigh two possible pieces of evidence to select the stronger.
developmental_invitations.use_when: The learner has several options or is over-citing.
developmental_invitations.avoid_when: There is no evidence yet to weigh.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Voice the doubting reader's objection to the evidence.
developmental_invitations.use_when: The learner assumes the evidence is self-evidently convincing.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Ask the learner to explain HOW the evidence bears on the claim (hand toward Explanation).
developmental_invitations.use_when: Relevant evidence sits unconnected.
developmental_invitations.avoid_when: Relevance itself is the problem — fix that first.

developmental_invitations.purpose: Have the learner state, in their own words, what makes evidence strong here.
developmental_invitations.use_when: Consolidating a gain.
developmental_invitations.avoid_when: The learner is still misjudging a dimension.

followup_decisions.after: Learner shows the evidence is off-claim and finds a relevant piece.
followup_decisions.consider: continue — now check sufficiency, then hand to Explanation for the connection.

followup_decisions.after: Learner narrows the claim to match a single case.
followup_decisions.consider: continue — verify the narrowed claim still answers the task.
change_target to Explanation/Analysis — evidence is no longer the bottleneck.

followup_decisions.after: Learner keeps treating an anecdote as proof.
followup_decisions.consider: increase_support — offer compare_candidates or make the illustration-vs-proof distinction explicit.

followup_decisions.after: Learner independently selects and represents evidence well.
followup_decisions.consider: conclude this target — consolidate and release.

followup_decisions.after: The underlying claim turns out to be the real weakness.
followup_decisions.consider: change_target to Central Claim/Thesis — do not teach evidence for an unworthy claim.

revision_strategies: Replace off-claim/background information with evidence about the claim's actual point.
Right-size the fit: narrow the claim to what the evidence carries, or add representative evidence.
Upgrade the grounds a skeptical reader would trust for this genre; drop popularity/hearsay.
Return to the source and correct any overstatement or out-of-context use.
Select the single strongest piece and cut redundant citations, then develop it.
Follow each retained piece with one sentence stating what it proves (bridge to Explanation).
stopping_conditions: Learner independently selects relevant, sufficient, credible, accurately-represented evidence and can say what it proves.
Diminishing returns — the evidence substantially earns the claim for the intended reader.
The connection (not the evidence) is now the bottleneck -> move to Explanation.
The claim itself is the bottleneck -> move to Central Claim/Thesis.
Learner requests independence; or teacher override designates another focus.

transfer.other_genres: The relevance/sufficiency/credibility/accuracy test persists; only the KIND of admissible evidence changes by genre.
transfer.other_assignments: The habit of asking 'what would give a doubting reader grounds to believe THIS claim?' applies to any argument.
transfer.other_disciplines: Standards of evidence differ (textual, documentary, empirical); the learner learns to ask what each field will accept.
transfer.future_writing: Foundational for research, professional reports, and any writing where conclusions must be earned, not asserted.

engine_usage.reader_function/writer_function: target selection + interpretation (why evidence matters now, from the reader's grounds)
engine_usage.functional_relationships: target selection — is EVIDENCE the bottleneck vs. the claim (upstream) or the explanation (downstream)
engine_usage.evidence_quality_dimensions: diagnostics — score relevance/sufficiency/credibility/accuracy SEPARATELY and pick the one failing dimension
engine_usage.common_difficulties/recognition_diagnost: diagnostics — name what the learner is attempting + the specific fault
engine_usage.look_alike_distinctions: diagnostics + invitation — resolve same-looking cases that need different teaching (false positives/negatives)
engine_usage.productive_misconceptions: instructional invitation — turn an evidence error into a stepping stone
engine_usage.genre_variation: diagnostics + interpretation — calibrate the credibility/sufficiency bar to the genre
engine_usage.developmental_invitations: instructional invitation — choose ONE type matched to the failing dimension (honor use_when/avoid_when)
engine_usage.followup_decisions: instructional decision — continue / retarget (claim or explanation) / +support / conclude

instructional_objects.definition: Reasoning that shows the reader what information means and how it contributes to the writer's larger point.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Make explicit what evidence means and how it establishes the claim.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the fact, example, quotation, or observation; interpret it; explain relevant relationships; connect it to the claim; clarify why the connection matters.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the student merely report or summarize? Are logical steps omitted? Is the connection between evidence and claim assumed rather than explained?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Reports/summarizes instead of interpreting; omits logical steps; assumes rather than explains the evidence-claim link.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask, “What does this show?” followed by, “How does that help establish your claim?” Guide the student through missing reasoning one step at a time.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student independently interprets evidence, makes reasoning explicit, and develops implications rather than relying on assertion.

instructional_objects.definition: A particular case used to clarify, illustrate, test, or support a general idea.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Make an abstract idea understandable through a representative case.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the idea needing illustration; choose a representative case; provide enough detail to make it understandable; explain how the example illustrates the idea.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is the idea too abstract for the reader? Is the example relevant and representative? Has the student explained what it demonstrates?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Idea left too abstract; example irrelevant/unrepresentative; student doesn't explain what it demonstrates.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to provide a concrete case and identify exactly which features of the case illustrate the larger idea.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student chooses purposeful examples, explains their relevance, and recognizes when one example is insufficient or unrepresentative.

instructional_objects.definition: A plausible alternative claim, objection, interpretation, or concern that challenges the writer's position.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Represent a genuine opposing view fairly so the argument can engage it.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify a genuine point of disagreement; represent it accurately and fairly; explain the reasoning behind it; show why it matters to the argument.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is there a meaningful alternative perspective? Has it been ignored, caricatured, or reduced to an easily defeated objection?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Opposing view ignored, caricatured, or reduced to a straw man.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what a thoughtful person might question or see differently. Help the student articulate the strongest reasonable version of that view.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student anticipates substantive objections, represents them charitably, and uses them to deepen rather than merely defend the argument.

instructional_objects.definition: The writer's reasoned answer to a counterargument or objection.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Answer an objection while acknowledging what is valid in it.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Acknowledge the counterargument; identify what is valid within it; explain its limits, errors, or different assumptions; revise or defend the original claim as needed.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the response address the actual objection? Does it dismiss rather than engage? Should the original claim be qualified instead of simply defended?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Dismisses instead of engaging; misses the actual objection; defends when the claim should be qualified.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what the counterargument gets right and where its reasoning no longer applies. Invite the student to refine the original position.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student responds directly, incorporates valid criticism, and strengthens or qualifies claims through engagement with alternatives.

instructional_objects.definition: Language that limits or specifies a claim so that it says no more and no less than the evidence supports.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Calibrate a claim's scope and certainty to what the evidence supports.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the claim's boundaries; consider exceptions and uncertainty; specify conditions, groups, degree, probability, or timeframe; choose language that reflects those limits.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is the claim absolute, sweeping, or more certain than the evidence permits? Is it so qualified that it says almost nothing?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Claim too absolute for the evidence; or so hedged it says nothing.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask, “Is this always true? For whom, under what conditions, and to what degree?” Help the student revise the claim's scope.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student calibrates claims to evidence, uses qualifications purposefully, and distinguishes reasonable precision from unnecessary hedging.

instructional_objects.definition: An examination of meaningful similarities between two or more subjects.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Use meaningful similarities to support interpretation or argument.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Establish the basis of comparison; select relevant dimensions; describe each subject using the same dimensions; explain the significance of the similarities.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Are the subjects genuinely comparable? Are equivalent dimensions used? Does the student merely list similarities without explaining their importance?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Subjects not genuinely comparable; unequal dimensions; similarities listed without significance.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what common question can be asked about both subjects and why the resulting similarity matters.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student selects illuminating comparison dimensions and uses similarities to support interpretation or argument.

instructional_objects.definition: An examination of meaningful differences between two or more subjects.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Draw warranted conclusions from significant differences.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Establish the basis of contrast; compare the subjects along equivalent dimensions; identify significant differences; explain what follows from those differences.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Are differences listed randomly? Are unlike features being compared? Is the significance of the contrast unclear?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Random difference-listing; comparing unlike features; unclear significance.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to compare both subjects on one shared dimension and explain why the difference matters.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student constructs balanced contrasts and draws warranted conclusions from significant differences.

instructional_objects.definition: An account of how and why one condition, event, or process contributes to another.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Explain the mechanism by which one thing produces another.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the proposed cause and outcome; explain the mechanism connecting them; consider contributing conditions, alternative causes, sequence, and evidence; avoid confusing correlation with causation.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is causation asserted without a mechanism? Are multiple causes reduced to one? Could the relationship be reversed, coincidental, or mediated by another factor?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Causation asserted without mechanism; multiple causes reduced to one; correlation mistaken for causation.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask, “By what process would this produce that result?” Help the student identify intermediate steps and competing explanations.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student explains causal mechanisms, considers interacting causes, and qualifies causal conclusions according to the evidence.

instructional_objects.definition: The organization of examples into meaningful groups based on shared criteria.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Group cases by a consistent principle to make them intelligible.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the purpose of grouping; establish a consistent criterion; define each category; assign examples according to the criterion; address overlap or borderline cases.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Are categories based on one clear principle? Do they overlap unnecessarily? Are important cases omitted or forced into unsuitable groups?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Inconsistent grouping principle; overlapping categories; forced or omitted cases.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what feature is being used to sort the examples and whether that feature is applied consistently to every case.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student creates purposeful, coherent categories and revises them when examples reveal ambiguity or overlap.

instructional_objects.definition: Language or structure that helps readers understand how one idea, sentence, paragraph, or section relates to another.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Show the reader the real relationship between ideas.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Determine the actual relationship between ideas; express that relationship through wording, repetition, sentence structure, or sequencing; provide enough guidance without mechanical labeling.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Can the reader follow the shift? Is the relationship additive, contrasting, causal, sequential, illustrative, or concessive? Is the transition word inaccurate or superficial?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Reader can't follow the shift; transition word inaccurate or superficial; mechanical labeling.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to state the relationship between the two ideas in ordinary language, then express that relationship in the writing.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student creates transitions based on genuine conceptual relationships and uses them flexibly without relying on a stock list.

instructional_objects.definition: A sentence that identifies the central contribution a paragraph makes to the surrounding discussion.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Tell the reader the single contribution the paragraph makes and connect it to the thesis.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Establish the paragraph's focus; state or imply its principal claim or function; connect it to the thesis or preceding discussion; prepare the reader for the paragraph's development.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the sentence merely announce a topic? Does it accurately represent the paragraph? Is the paragraph's contribution clear without it?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Merely announces a topic; doesn't represent the paragraph; no clear contribution.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask, “What single idea does this paragraph help the reader understand?” Help the student state that idea in relation to the larger argument.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: Topic sentences increasingly express meaningful claims, orient the reader, and accurately govern paragraph development.

instructional_objects.definition: Specific information that develops, clarifies, illustrates, or supports a paragraph's central idea.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Develop a paragraph's claim with functionally relevant specifics.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Determine what the paragraph's claim requires; add relevant facts, examples, descriptions, quotations, or reasoning; explain their relationship to the central idea.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is the paragraph underdeveloped? Are details relevant, sufficient, and ordered? Do they support the main idea or merely concern the same topic?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Underdeveloped; details merely on-topic rather than supporting the point; poorly ordered.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what the reader still needs to know or understand to accept the paragraph's main point.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student selects and organizes details according to their function rather than accumulating loosely related information.

instructional_objects.definition: A sentence that completes a paragraph's work and helps the reader understand its significance or connection to what follows.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Complete a paragraph's work and mark its significance or link to what follows.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Synthesize the paragraph's contribution; state its implication; connect it to the larger claim or next idea; avoid merely repeating the topic sentence.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the paragraph end abruptly? Does the final sentence add significance or simply restate earlier wording? Is closure actually needed?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Ends abruptly; restates the topic sentence; unnecessary closure.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask, “What should the reader now understand because of this paragraph?” Invite the student to express that implication.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student closes paragraphs selectively and purposefully, emphasizing implications or movement in the argument.

instructional_objects.definition: A group of related sentences that develops one coherent contribution to a larger piece of writing.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Develop one coherent contribution to the larger text.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Establish a central purpose or claim; orient the reader; develop the idea through explanation, evidence, and examples; organize sentences logically; connect the paragraph to the larger text.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the paragraph have one governing purpose? Are sentences relevant and coherently ordered? Is it adequately developed? Should it be divided or combined?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: No single governing purpose; irrelevant/disordered sentences; under- or over-developed.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to state the paragraph's job in the essay and examine how each sentence contributes to that job.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student constructs unified, developed paragraphs of flexible length and organizes them according to meaning rather than formula.

instructional_objects.definition: The opening section that brings readers into the subject, establishes the writing situation, and prepares them for the essay's central direction.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Bring the reader into the subject and prepare them for the central claim.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Engage attention appropriately; introduce the subject and problem; provide necessary context; establish relevance; clarify key terms when needed; lead toward the thesis or controlling purpose.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the reader understand the subject, stakes, and direction? Is context missing or excessive? Is the opening generic, disconnected, or overly broad?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Reader lacks subject/stakes/direction; context missing or excessive; generic or overly broad opening.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what the intended reader must know before encountering the thesis and what would make the problem worth attending to.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student adapts introductions to audience and purpose, selects relevant context, and creates a coherent path toward the central claim.

instructional_objects.definition: An opening that gives the reader a meaningful reason to attend to the subject.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Give the reader a genuine, relevant reason to care about the subject.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify what is interesting, puzzling, consequential, vivid, or contested about the subject; present it accurately; connect it directly to the essay's purpose.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the opening create relevant interest or merely use a decorative question, quotation, or dramatic statement? Is its connection to the essay clear?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Decorative/generic hook; unclear connection to the essay.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what is genuinely surprising, important, or unresolved about the topic and help the student begin there.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student creates varied, relevant openings and abandons formulaic hooks that do not serve the essay.

instructional_objects.definition: Information readers need in order to understand the subject, problem, concepts, or argument that follows.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Supply the minimum knowledge the reader needs to understand what follows.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify what the intended reader likely knows; supply necessary history, circumstances, definitions, or debate; select only information that prepares the reader for the central discussion.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: What knowledge is being assumed? Is essential information missing? Is the writer providing an unfocused history or facts that do not support understanding?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Assumes knowledge the reader lacks; missing essentials; unfocused history/facts.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what the reader must understand before the main claim will make sense, then identify the minimum sufficient context.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student anticipates audience knowledge and provides focused context without overwhelming or distracting the reader.

instructional_objects.definition: The closing section that completes the essay's work by clarifying what has been established and why it matters.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Complete the essay by clarifying what was established and why it matters.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Return to the central problem or claim; synthesize rather than merely repeat; draw implications; acknowledge remaining questions or limits when appropriate; provide meaningful closure.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the conclusion merely restate the thesis and main points? Does it introduce unsupported new claims? Does it explain the significance of the essay's reasoning?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Merely restates the thesis; introduces unsupported new claims; no significance.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask, “What can the reader now understand that was not clear at the beginning, and why does that matter?”
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student produces conclusions that synthesize reasoning, articulate implications, and provide closure suited to the essay's purpose.

instructional_objects.definition: A brief name for a piece of writing that identifies or frames its subject and invites appropriate expectations.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Frame the subject and set appropriate reader expectations.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the central subject and angle; select precise and engaging language; signal genre, argument, or focus when useful; avoid titles that are vague or misleading.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the title reflect the actual essay? Is it overly general, decorative, or simply the assignment label?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Overly general/decorative; just the assignment label; misleading.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to name both the subject and what the essay says or reveals about it.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: Titles become more precise, purposeful, original, and aligned with the completed writing.

instructional_objects.definition: A linguistically complete unit that expresses a thought, action, relationship, question, or command.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Express one clear thought whose relationships the reader can follow.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Establish a subject or focus; express an action, state, or relationship; organize clauses and modifiers so their relationships are clear; punctuate the resulting structure appropriately.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Can the reader identify who or what the sentence concerns and what is being said? Is it fragmented, fused, overloaded, ambiguous, or syntactically confusing?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Fragmented/fused/overloaded/ambiguous syntax; unclear subject or assertion.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to identify the central actor or topic and the main action or assertion, then rebuild the sentence around that relationship.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student creates increasingly varied, controlled sentences and revises syntax according to meaning, emphasis, and reader comprehension.

instructional_objects.definition: The selection of words that express the writer's intended meaning with appropriate precision, force, and tone.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Convey the intended meaning with precision, force, and appropriate tone.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Determine the exact meaning; choose words suited to audience and context; prefer concrete and specific language where useful; test connotations; remove unnecessary or misleading wording.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is the wording vague, inaccurate, repetitive, inflated, informal, or inconsistent with the intended meaning? Would a different word materially improve understanding?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Vague/inaccurate/inflated/informal wording; connotations unmanaged.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what the student means in ordinary language, then compare the current word with the intended meaning.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student chooses increasingly precise language, notices connotation, and revises wording based on meaning rather than superficial variety.

instructional_objects.definition: The stance or attitude toward the subject and reader conveyed through language and presentation.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Establish the intended relationship with the reader through consistent stance.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the relationship the writer wants with the reader; choose vocabulary, syntax, level of certainty, detail, and formality consistent with that relationship; maintain or deliberately vary the stance.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the tone suit the audience, purpose, and subject? Does it shift unintentionally? Is it dismissive, exaggerated, detached, or falsely authoritative?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Tone unsuited to audience/purpose; unintentional shifts; dismissive/exaggerated/falsely authoritative.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask how the writer wants the reader to experience the voice and identify one wording choice that supports or undermines that relationship.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student deliberately adjusts tone across contexts and explains how particular language choices create that tone.

instructional_objects.definition: Attention to what intended readers know, need, value, expect, or may misunderstand.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Shape explanations, evidence, organization, and tone to the real reader's knowledge and needs.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify likely readers; estimate their knowledge and perspectives; anticipate questions and points of confusion; select explanations, evidence, organization, and tone accordingly.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is the student writing only from personal understanding? What knowledge, assumptions, or responses are attributed to the reader without justification?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Writes only from personal understanding; unjustified assumptions about the reader.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to imagine a particular reader and identify the first question or confusion that reader might have.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student anticipates reader needs throughout composing and adapts writing flexibly for different audiences.

instructional_objects.definition: The purposeful arrangement of ideas and sections so that the reader can follow the development of the writing.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Arrange ideas so the reader can follow the development of the writing.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Identify the overall task; determine the major ideas or stages required; group related material; order groups according to logic and reader need; establish relationships among sections.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is there a discernible progression? Are ideas grouped and sequenced purposefully? Does the organization reflect the argument or merely the order in which ideas occurred?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: No discernible progression; ideas ordered by occurrence rather than logic/reader need.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to name the major jobs the essay must perform and arrange them in the order the reader needs.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student creates and revises organizational plans based on conceptual relationships, purpose, and reader understanding.

instructional_objects.definition: The quality by which ideas fit together into an understandable and continuous line of thought.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Keep the line of thought continuous and followable for the reader.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Maintain a clear focus; establish logical and semantic relationships; order information purposefully; use transitions, repeated concepts, and consistent terminology; resolve unexplained shifts.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Can the reader explain how each idea follows from the previous one? Are relationships missing, contradictory, or dependent on unstated assumptions?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Missing/contradictory relationships; unexplained shifts; reliance on unstated assumptions.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Select one confusing shift and ask the student to state the relationship between the ideas explicitly.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student anticipates where readers may lose the line of thought and creates coherence through reasoning and structure, not transition words alone.

instructional_objects.definition: The condition in which all parts of a passage contribute to a shared central purpose or idea.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Keep every part of a passage serving one governing purpose.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Establish the governing purpose; include material that develops it; remove, relocate, or reframe material that does not; ensure each part has a discernible function.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Do all sentences or sections contribute to the same central work? Is material merely related to the topic rather than relevant to the purpose?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Material merely on-topic rather than serving the purpose; digressions retained.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to identify the passage's job and explain how each sentence helps perform it. Examine the first sentence that does not.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student independently detects digressions, maintains focus, and reorganizes useful material rather than retaining it merely because it is interesting.

instructional_objects.definition: The recognizable presence or perspective of the writer expressed through choices of language, emphasis, reasoning, and stance.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Maintain an authentic authorial presence while meeting the demands of the context.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Develop ideas the writer genuinely understands and can stand behind; make deliberate language and tone choices; express judgments with appropriate confidence; integrate sources without surrendering authorship.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Does the writing sound generic, borrowed, mechanical, or unlike the student's demonstrated understanding? Is personal voice replacing disciplined reasoning, or has formal language erased the writer's agency?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Generic/borrowed/mechanical voice; voice replacing reasoning, or formality erasing agency.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to explain the idea aloud in their own words, then revise the passage while preserving that meaning and meeting the demands of the context.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student maintains an identifiable perspective while adapting appropriately to genre, evidence, audience, and academic conventions.

instructional_objects.definition: The purposeful reworking of writing to improve what it communicates and how effectively it does so.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Rework writing to better serve purpose, meaning, structure, and reader.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Reconsider purpose and task; evaluate reader understanding; examine global organization and central claims; revise paragraphs and reasoning; refine sentences and words; proofread after substantive changes.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is revision limited to correction and word substitution? Does the student recognize mismatches among purpose, meaning, structure, and reader response?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Revision limited to correction/word swaps; mismatches among purpose/meaning/structure/reader unnoticed.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Choose one high-leverage issue connected to the essay's purpose. Ask the student to make a meaningful change and compare the effect of the two versions.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student rereads from a reader's perspective, identifies consequential problems, makes substantive changes, and explains why revisions improve the writing.

instructional_objects.definition: An explanation of what a word, idea, or concept means in the present context.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Make an important concept understandable to the intended reader.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: State the concept's basic meaning; identify its defining qualities; explain unfamiliar words within the explanation; distinguish it from related concepts when useful; elaborate until the intended reader can understand it.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is an important concept unexplained? Would the intended reader understand the explanation? Is it circular, vague, overly broad, overly narrow, or merely an example?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Important concept left unexplained; circular/vague/over-broad/over-narrow; example given instead of definition.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask the student to explain the concept in ordinary language. Identify one unclear word or idea in that explanation and invite further elaboration.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student recognizes when a concept requires explanation and constructs appropriately complete definitions for different audiences and purposes.

instructional_objects.definition: A general idea used to organize and interpret particular examples, experiences, or events.
instructional_objects.communicative_purpose: Give the reader an organizing idea that governs particular cases.
instructional_objects.performance_structure: Name the idea; identify the qualities that make something an instance of it; distinguish central from incidental features; connect examples to the general idea; clarify its boundaries.
instructional_objects.recognition_diagnostics: Is the student using a term without understanding it? Are examples confused with the concept? Are defining qualities missing or inconsistent?
instructional_objects.common_obstacles: Term used without understanding; examples confused with the concept; inconsistent defining qualities.
instructional_objects.next_developmental_moves: Ask what different examples have in common and what would not count as an example. Help the student state the general idea.
instructional_objects.indicators_of_control: The student explains concepts abstractly, identifies valid and invalid examples, and uses concepts consistently in new contexts.
